correctness.rationale: For \(0<t\le1\), the identity \(I+\sigma P=(I+\sigma tP)+\sigma(1-t)P\) forces the sharp lower bound, while the triangle inequality gives the matching upper bound. For \(t\ge1\), the decomposition \(I+\sigma P=t^{-1}(I+\sigma tP)+(1-t^{-1})I\) does the same. Every rank-one \(T=f\otimes x\) satisfies \(T^2=f(x)T\); if the scalar is nonzero, \(P=T/f(x)\) is a projection and \(T^2=f(x)^2P\), a positive multiple over the real field. Thus the projection hypothesis yields Langemets’s signed-square property for every rank-one operator, which characterizes Daugavet in real dimension greater than one.

value.rationale: The theorem isolates a natural exact projection boundary: a single-scale equality on rank-one idempotents suffices, while the classical bad-projection inequality is strictly weaker. This makes the newest square characterization easier to test on a distinguished operator class.
residual_risks: The scalar field is real and dimension exceeds one.
No complex analogue follows from the same fixed-sign hypothesis.

final_claim: For every real Banach space of dimension greater than one and either fixed sign \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), the Daugavet property is equivalent to \(\|I+\sigma P\|=1+\|P\|\) for every rank-one projection \(P\); the scale-one identity automatically propagates to every \(t>0\).
